runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its twelve GAI-specific risks, in Section 2.4 on page 11. Its main points are:

- **Training data as the source of exposure.** The profile says the risk starts with training. Model builders often don't say which data they used, so users can't tell whether personal information went into training or how it was gathered. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation. Most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.

- **Leaking training data.** The profile reports that memorized training content can come out. During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. It adds that this may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

- **Inferring personal information.** Privacy exposure is not limited to data the model was trained on. GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. The profile notes that such inferences can cause harm even when they are wrong, since these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations).

- **Downstream harms.** The profile links privacy harms to other harms, such as adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

The profile also cross-references data privacy in its discussion of jailbreaking and information security, noting that output restrictions may not hold against new prompts and that this is also relevant to CBRN Information or Capabilities, Data Privacy, Information Security, and Obscene, Degrading and/or Abusive Content.

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its twelve GAI-specific risks, in Section 2.4 on page 11. Its main points are:

- **Training data as the source of exposure.** The profile says the risk starts with training. Model builders often don't say which data they used, so users can't tell whether personal information went into training or how it was gathered. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation. Most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.

- **Leaking training data.** The profile reports that memorized training content can come out. During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. It adds that this may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

- **Inferring personal information.** Privacy exposure is not limited to data the model was trained on. GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. The profile notes that such inferences can cause harm even when they are wrong, since these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations).

- **Downstream harms.** The profile links privacy harms to other harms, such as adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

The profile also cross-references data privacy in its discussion of jailbreaking and information security, noting that output restrictions may not hold against new prompts and that this is also relevant to CBRN Information or Capabilities, Data Privacy, Information Security, and Obscene, Degrading and/or Abusive Content.

segments.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its twelve GAI-specific risks, in Section 2.4 on page 11. Its main points are:

- **Training data as the source of exposure.** The profile says the risk starts with training. Model builders often don't say which data they used, so users can't tell whether personal information went into training or how it was gathered.
The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation.

Most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.
- **Leaking training data.** The profile reports that memorized training content can come out.
During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data.
It adds that this
may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.
- **Inferring personal information.** Privacy exposure is not limited to data the model was trained on.
GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources.
The profile notes that such inferences can cause harm even when they are wrong, since
these inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations)

.

- **Downstream harms.** The profile links privacy harms to other harms, such as
adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups

.

The profile also cross-references data privacy in its discussion of jailbreaking and information security, noting that output restrictions may not hold against new prompts and that this is
also relevant to CBRN Information or Capabilities, Data Privacy, Information Security, and Obscene, Degrading and/or Abusive Content

.
